```{r fig-clusters-k4}
            show.legend = FALSE, colour = INK_SECONDARY) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = PAL_CAT[1:4]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " pp")) + pct_axis() +
  labs(title = "A four-way split, offered as description rather than as a finding",
       subtitle = "Same features, k = 4. The silhouette barely improves on k = 2, so read these as labels on a continuum",
       x = "Race gap, widest minus narrowest of the three largest groups",
       y = "Overall obesity rate")

gg_live(g)
```

```{r cluster4-table}
tbl(profile4 |> transmute(Profile = label4, States = n,
                          `Obesity (%)` = round(obesity, 1),
                          `Income gap (pp)` = round(income_gap, 1),
                          `Race gap (pp)` = round(race_gap, 1),
                          `Trend (pp/yr)` = round(trend_pp, 2)),
    caption = "The four-way profiles")
```

The four-way version separates two groups that a policymaker would treat
differently. A high-obesity, narrow-gap state has a population-wide problem and
should be reached with population-wide measures. A high-obesity, wide-gap state
has a targeting problem, where the same total burden is distributed very unevenly
and universal programmes will reach the wrong people first.

## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

**Race is the widest disparity and it is not moving.** At roughly 29 percentage
points nationally, the race and ethnicity gap is three times the income gap and
two and a half times the education gap, and fourteen years of data show no trend
in it. @sec-importance and @sec-incremental agree from two different directions:
of the dimensions that constitute a social disparity, race carries the most
explanatory weight. The caveat in @sec-gaps stands, that the 29-point figure is
driven by Asian adults at the low end and the gap among the three largest groups
is closer to 10 points, and both numbers belong in any honest summary.

**The income convergence is not real.** This is the finding an analysis could most
easily get wrong. Read at face value, the income gap fell by 72% between 2011 and
2024 and the natural conclusion is that income-based disparity in obesity has
nearly disappeared. @sec-break shows that the 2021 BRFSS income question redesign
moved twenty percentage points of respondents out of the top bracket, and that the
top bracket's measured prevalence jumped 4.7 points in the same year as a
consequence. Within a single instrument regime the gap is roughly flat. The
diagnostic that caught this is simple and general: watch the composition of a
stratification variable over time, and treat a large jump as an instrument change
until proven otherwise.

**Forecasts extend the trend but do not close the gaps.** National prevalence is
projected to reach roughly 36% by 2030 on either method. Neither gap is projected
to close. Both projections rest on fourteen observations and the backtest in
@sec-forecast shows the simpler linear method outperforming ARIMA on this data, so
the intervals rather than the point estimates are what should be quoted.

**Ecological inference is the binding limitation.** Every result here concerns
groups within states, not individuals. Nothing in this data can say what obesity
prevalence is among low-income Black adults in Alabama, because @sec-structure's
structural fact means the file never reports two demographic variables together.
The apparent independence of income and race in @sec-importance may therefore
reflect the data's structure rather than the world: income and race are correlated
in the US population, and an analysis that cannot see them together cannot
separate their effects. This is the single strongest argument for moving to BRFSS
individual-level microdata for any follow-up.

**The transformation assumptions are stated and tested.** The \$100,000 midpoint
for the open-ended top income bracket and the 75-year midpoint for "65 or older"
are estimates, not observations. @sec-sensitivity refits both relationships across
a plausible range and no conclusion changes.

**Other caveats.** BRFSS height and weight are self-reported, and self-reported
BMI is known to understate obesity, so every level in this report is likely a
floor rather than a point estimate. Suppression is concentrated in the smallest
racial and ethnic groups, so state-level race results are systematically thinner
for the groups where disparities may be largest. Survey mode and weighting shifted
during 2020 and 2021. And state, income and race distributions are mutually
confounded: a state-level association between race and obesity partly reflects
which states particular populations live in.

## Conclusion and recommendations {#sec-conclusion}

The gap that matters most in US adult obesity is racial, it is about 29 percentage
points wide, and it has not narrowed in fourteen years. The income gap, which a
face-value reading would report as having nearly closed, has not closed either;
the appearance of convergence is an artefact of a survey instrument change in 2021.
Both models and both forecasting methods agree that current trajectories carry
national prevalence to roughly 36% by 2030 with the gaps intact.

Three practical implications follow.

1. **Target by race and geography together, not by income alone.** Income is the
   weakest of the three social dimensions measured here, explaining
   `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * incr$incremental[incr$dimension == "Income"])` of
   within-stratum variance against
   `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * incr$incremental[incr$dimension == "Race / ethnicity"])`
   for race. The state clusters in @sec-cluster separate places with a
   population-wide problem from places with a distributional one, and those two
   situations call for different programmes.
2. **Treat the flat race gap as evidence that current approaches are not working
   on it.** Fourteen years of rising prevalence with a constant gap means every
   group is getting worse at roughly the same rate. Interventions that lift all
   groups equally will not close it; only something that acts differentially will.
3. **Fix the income series before using it for policy.** Any analysis of BRFSS
   income trends spanning 2021 needs to handle the break explicitly. The
   composition diagnostic in @sec-break takes about ten lines of code and should be
   standard practice on any long survey panel.

**Next steps.** Three extensions would materially strengthen this work. BRFSS
individual-level microdata would remove the ecological inference limit and allow
income and race to be modelled jointly, which is the question this data cannot
answer. External predictors such as food access, healthcare access and physical
activity infrastructure would move the analysis from description toward
explanation; the same BRFSS release carries physical activity and nutrition
questions that were not used here. And a county-level or census-tract analysis
would replace the 55-jurisdiction geography with something fine enough to site an
actual intervention.

---

**Data source.** Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, *Nutrition, Physical
Activity, and Obesity - Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System*, accessed via
